lead: The connecting rod links the piston to the crank, and the crankshaft turns the rod’s push into torque. The rod is a column that can buckle, with a bearing at each end; the crankshaft is a shaft under bending and twisting whose worst load changes as it turns. Design takes the peak gas force, sizes the rod as a column and its ends for bearing pressure, then checks the crankshaft in the two positions that load it most.
prereq: You need: combined bending and torsion from shafts under bending, torsion and axial loads, and Rankine’s column formula from strength of materials.

sections.h3: Forces on the connecting rod and its I-section

blocks.text: The peak gas force on the piston is F<sub>p</sub> = (π/4)D²p<sub>max</sub>, with D the bore and p<sub>max</sub> the peak cylinder pressure. Near top dead centre, where p<sub>max</sub> acts, the rod is almost in line with the cylinder, so the rod force F<sub>c</sub> = F<sub>p</sub>/cos φ is taken as F<sub>p</sub> (φ is the rod’s angle to the cylinder axis). The rod is then a strut that can buckle.

Rods of high-speed engines use an I-section of web and flange thickness t, width B = 4t and depth H = 5t. Then A = 11t², Ixx = 419t⁴/12, Iyy = 131t⁴/12 and kxx² = Ixx/A = 3.17t². In the plane of motion the rod is pinned at both ends (buckling about xx, length L); out of that plane its ends are nearly fixed (about yy, length L/2). Equal strength needs Ixx = 4Iyy; the I-section gives 3.2, so it is designed about xx.

Pcr = σc A/(1 + a(L/kxx)²)
Rankine’s formula: σc is the crushing stress (about 330 MPa for steel), a = 1/7500 for steel, L the rod length between centres. Take Pcr = (factor of safety) × Fp, with 5 to 6 for rods.

The depth H is usually tapered: about 1.1H to 1.25H at the big end and 0.75H to 0.9H at the small end. At high speed the rod’s own mass swings sideways and bends it (whipping); the largest inertia bending moment is M = m ω²rL²/(9√3), with m the rod mass per unit length and r the crank radius. Some syllabi ask for this check.

sections.h3: Small end, big end and cap bolts

blocks.text: Each end is a plain bearing sized for bearing pressure p<sub>b</sub>: F<sub>p</sub> = d l p<sub>b</sub>, with d the pin diameter and l its length. The small end (piston pin) runs slowly and oscillates, so typical values are p<sub>b</sub> ≈ 12 to 15 MPa with l/d ≈ 1.5 to 2; the big end (crankpin) takes about 10 MPa with l/d ≈ 1.0 to 1.25. The big-end cap bolts carry the inertia force of the piston and rod at top dead centre of the exhaust stroke, F<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>r</sub> ω² r(1 + 1/n<sub>r</sub>), where m<sub>r</sub> is the reciprocating mass and n<sub>r</sub> = L/r; they are sized on their core area in tension.
A centre crankshaft has the crankpin between two main bearings; an overhung (side) crankshaft has it outside one bearing. A crankshaft is checked in two positions:

items: Crank at top dead centre: the full gas force acts on the crankpin with no torque. Find the bearing reactions, then size the crankpin by bearing pressure (Fp = dc lc pb) and check it in bending, M = R1 b1, σb = 32M/(πdc³). The webs see direct compression plus bending.

Crank at the angle of maximum torque (about 25° to 35° after top dead centre): the rod force splits into a tangential part Ft, which gives the torque Ft r, and a radial part Fr. Here the crankpin and the shaft next to the web carry bending and torsion together, and the equivalent torque √(M² + T²) gives the diameter.

blocks.text: The shaft under the flywheel is checked for the flywheel weight and belt pull in bending plus the torque. Generous pin-web fillets keep the stress concentration down.

examples.question: Design the I-section of a steel connecting rod for an engine with bore 100 mm, peak gas pressure 4 MPa and rod length 240 mm between centres. Take a factor of safety of 6, σ<sub>c</sub> = 330 MPa and a = 1/7500. Also find the small-end pin and big-end crankpin sizes for p<sub>b</sub> = 12.5 MPa with l/d = 2 and p<sub>b</sub> = 10 MPa with l/d = 1.
steps: Simplify: 3630t² = 188 496 + 456 070/t², so 3630t⁴ − 188 496t² − 456 060 = 0. Solving the quadratic in t² gives t² = 54.24 mm², t = 7.37 mm.
Adopt t = 8 mm: B = 32 mm, H = 40 mm, A = 704 mm², k<sub>xx</sub>² = 203.2 mm². Then P<sub>cr</sub> = 330 × 704/(1 + 240²/(7500 × 203.2)) = 223 860 N, a factor of safety of 7.1.
Small end: d² = F<sub>p</sub>/(2p<sub>b</sub>) = 31 416/(2 × 12.5) = 1257 mm², d = 35.4 mm; adopt 36 mm × 72 mm.
Big end: d² = F<sub>p</sub>/p<sub>b</sub> = 31 416/10 = 3142 mm², d = 56.0 mm; adopt 56 mm × 56 mm.
examples.answer: I-section t = 8 mm, B = 32 mm, H = 40 mm (about 44 to 50 mm at the big end, 30 to 36 mm at the small end); piston pin 36 × 72 mm; crankpin 56 × 56 mm.

examples.question: The same engine has a centre crankshaft with the crankpin centre 100 mm from each main bearing centre. With the crank at top dead centre and the gas force of 31 416 N on the crankpin, check the 56 mm crankpin in bending for an allowable stress of 75 MPa, and resize it if needed. Ignore the flywheel.
steps: Reactions: by symmetry R<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>2</sub> = 31 416/2 = 15 708 N.
Bending moment at the crankpin centre: M = R<sub>1</sub> × 100 = 1 570 800 N·mm.
Stress at d<sub>c</sub> = 56 mm: σ<sub>b</sub> = 32M/(πd<sub>c</sub>³) = 32 × 1 570 800/(π × 56³) = 91.1 MPa, above 75 MPa.
Resize: d<sub>c</sub>³ = 32M/(π × 75) = 213 330 mm³, d<sub>c</sub> = 59.8 mm. Adopt 60 mm.
Check at 60 mm: σ<sub>b</sub> = 74.1 MPa ≤ 75 MPa; bearing pressure with l<sub>c</sub> = 60 mm: 31 416/(60 × 60) = 8.73 MPa ≤ 10 MPa.
examples.answer: The 56 mm crankpin chosen for bearing pressure fails in bending (91.1 MPa); a 60 mm × 60 mm crankpin passes both checks.

traps: Designing the rod for crushing (σ<sub>c</sub> A) alone. It is a column, so Rankine’s formula with the slenderness L/k<sub>xx</sub> sets the size.
Using k<sub>yy</sub> and length L together. Buckling about yy has equivalent length L/2; the I-section is designed about xx with length L.
Forgetting the factor of safety on the gas force before entering Rankine’s formula.
Sizing the crankpin by bearing pressure and stopping. At top dead centre it must also pass the bending check, as the second example shows.
Checking the crankshaft only at top dead centre. The maximum-torque position adds torsion and can govern the shaft next to the web.

quiz.q: Give the proportions and area of the I-section used for connecting rods.
quiz.a: Flange and web thickness t, width B = 4t, depth H = 5t; A = 11t².

quiz.q: Why is the connecting rod designed for buckling about the xx axis only?
quiz.a: In the plane of motion the rod is pinned at both ends (length L); out of that plane the ends are nearly fixed (length L/2). The I-section has I<sub>xx</sub> = 3.2I<sub>yy</sub>, close to the 4 that would make both equal, so buckling about xx governs.

quiz.q: In which two positions is a crankshaft checked?
quiz.a: At top dead centre (maximum bending, no torque) and at the crank angle of maximum torque (bending plus torsion).

quiz.q: An engine has bore 80 mm and peak pressure 5 MPa. Find the gas force and the crankpin diameter for p<sub>b</sub> = 10 MPa and l/d = 1.
For t = 8 mm, L = 240 mm, σ<sub>c</sub> = 330 MPa and a = 1/7500, find the Rankine buckling load of the I-section rod.
What is whipping of a connecting rod?
quiz.a: At high speed the rod’s own mass swings sideways and bends it like a beam; the largest moment is m ω²rL²/(9√3).

quiz.q: An engine is tuned to a higher peak pressure. Which design checks change, and why?
quiz.a: The gas force rises with p<sub>max</sub>. The rod’s buckling margin falls, so t must grow; both end bearings need more area for the same p<sub>b</sub>; and the crankpin bending at top dead centre rises, so the crankpin must grow.

beyond: Modern rods are forged or sintered and the big end is often fracture-split, so the cap fits back exactly. Crankshafts are checked by finite element analysis with the full gas and inertia loads over a cycle, and their fillets are rolled or induction hardened for fatigue strength. Search for "fracture split connecting rod" and "crankshaft fillet rolling".

figure.caption: The connecting rod of the first worked example. The I-section with t = 8 mm has B = 32 mm and H = 40 mm; the rod is a 240 mm strut carrying the 31.4 kN gas force. Pinned in the plane of motion, it is designed for buckling about x, and Rankine’s formula gives 223.9 kN, 7.1 times the gas force.
